messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tane, a seventy‑one‑year‑old painter from a coastal town in New Zealand, grew up sketching the dunes and fishing boats that defined his world. One sunny afternoon in his late fifties, he was at the town’s annual harvest festival when a sudden explosion shattered the air, turning bright laughter into screams. The shockwave left him on the ground, clutching his chest, as flames erupted in the pavilion. He watched the building collapse, the smell of smoke seared into his memory, and the sound of distant sirens became an indelible trigger. Even now, when the distant rumble of a truck or a sudden burst of music echoes, Tane’s body snaps back into the position he held during that terror: his hands clutch his ribs, his shoulders rigid, his breath shallow. The memory is not a passive recollection; it forces itself into his mind whenever he tries to avoid thinking about it, and its details— the crack of the roof, the black smoke— remain crystal clear. This unrelenting recollection convinces him that the world is a place where danger lurks behind every shadow and that he cannot rely on himself to stay safe. Because Tane feels unable to trust his own judgment, he constantly seeks reassurance from anyone who will listen. At work, he pauses before applying each color, asking the studio assistant if the hue is “right,” and he insists on hearing the same calm affirmation over and over. He also practices tight emotional control, swallowing anger and fear into a tightness in his chest, and refuses to leave the studio to buy new brushes or canvases, convinced that stepping outside could bring another catastrophe. His belief that others cannot protect him fuels this routine of reassurance seeking, emotional suppression, and avoidance of the outside world. The very act of repeating this routine keeps the memory fresh. Each time Tane asks for confirmation, he relives the moment of the explosion as if it were happening again; the same physical posture, the same gasp of breath. By continually rehearsing the scene, he reinforces the vividness of the memory, ensuring that the body’s automatic response remains a constant, involuntary echo whenever a trigger appears. The cycle of seeking reassurance and emotional control thus directly sustains the memory’s hold over his daily life. Simultaneously, these maladaptive strategies deepen his negative beliefs. When he cannot convince a friend that the streets are safe, he internalizes the notion that his own sense of safety is unreliable, and that no one else can provide that safety either. Each failed attempt at reassurance confirms that the world remains a hostile place, a place where even the smallest risk feels catastrophic. Consequently, his worldview tightens around the idea that he must remain in a controlled, isolated bubble, lest he be struck again. The weight of these beliefs has become a heavy cloak that drapes over every brushstroke. Tane has stopped canvassing the shoreline, fearing the waves might carry unseen threats. His paintings, once vibrant scenes of daily life, now seem to be silent reminders of a life interrupted. The avoidance of the streets and the relentless reassurance seeking have isolated him from the community he once loved, and his solitary studio has become a quiet witness to a mind in constant alarm. When Tane finally stepped into a counseling room, it was after a night of sleep deprivation and an afternoon spent staring at his blank canvas, feeling the weight of each brushstroke as a potential trigger. He was afraid that if he continued to live in this loop, he might never regain the ability to finish a painting, or worse, to step into a world he now perceived as unsafe. What he hopes for most is a way to quiet the unbidden memories, to trust his own judgment again, and to breathe freely, both on canvas and beyond.
